title: LaFlash: Capacity-Driven Acceleration for Coding Agent Workflows via QLC-HBF
summary: LaFlash replaces recomputation of evicted agent states (contexts and KV caches) with retention in a High-Bandwidth Flash tier built on QLC NAND, allocating memory between active concurrency and dormant-state storage via Session Grouping and Fast-Page Allocation. It requires specialized HBF hardware that does not exist in commodity GPU servers or API-based deployments, and its benefits depend on QLC's heterogeneous read latency and limited write endurance being managed through request-exclusive placement and HBM buffering. It can fail under highly irregular reactivation patterns that break read parallelism across session groups, or when write-intensive workloads exceed QLC endurance despite buffering.
rationale: The technique is a custom QLC flash memory architecture with hardware-level data placement, which is not deployable on a single 24 GB GPU or through third-party APIs, though its capacity-driven acceleration principle (retain dormant states instead of recomputing them) is worth tracking as NVMe-offload tooling matures.
technique: Capacity-driven KV/state retention on QLC flash

claims.statement: LaFlash replaces recomputation of evicted agent states (contexts and KV caches) with retention in a High-Bandwidth Flash tier built on QLC NAND, allocating memory between active concurrency and dormant-state storage via Session Grouping and Fast-Page Allocation. It requires specialized HBF hardware that does not exist in commodity GPU servers or API-based deployments, and its benefits depend on QLC's heterogeneous read latency and limited write endurance being managed through request-exclusive placement and HBM buffering. It can fail under highly irregular reactivation patterns that break read parallelism across session groups, or when write-intensive workloads exceed QLC endurance despite buffering.

LaFlash achieves 7.04x higher throughput and 10.96x higher energy efficiency over SLC-HBF with batch expansion, and 2.36x higher throughput over QLC-HBF with CDA (the like-for-like capacity-driven baseline) on end-to-end coding agent workloads.
